questions.prompt: Per the course's HTTP status code reference in Lesson 3, what does a 4xx-class status code indicate?
options: The client's request itself was invalid, unauthenticated, or not allowed
The server encountered an unexpected error while otherwise processing a valid request
The resource was found but the server wants you to look elsewhere for it
The request succeeded and returned the requested data
The request was received and is still being processed
The request succeeded but intentionally has no body to send back
questions.explain: The first digit of an HTTP status code sorts it into one of five classes, and the classes split cleanly by which side is at fault: 4xx means the client did something wrong — a malformed request, missing credentials, or a resource that doesn't exist. Recognizing the class from the first digit, before even reading the specific code, is the whole point of memorizing the five-class breakdown.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the 5xx class, not 4xx — that's the server's own fault (an unexpected failure handling an otherwise-valid request), the opposite side of the client/server line that 4xx draws. Mixing up which side is at fault is exactly the kind of mistake the five-class breakdown is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: A RESTful API requires the client to send its auth token on every single request, even seconds after the previous request already succeeded. Per Lesson 2, why?
options: Statelessness means the server remembers nothing about previous requests, so each request must carry everything the server needs, including authentication
It's a purely cosmetic convention with no functional purpose
Tokens automatically expire every few seconds, so a fresh one is always required
Only POST and PUT requests require the token; GET requests never need it
questions.explain: Statelessness is one of REST's three core ideas: the server does not remember anything about your previous request, so every request has to be entirely self-contained, auth included. This is also why any server in a pool can handle any request — nothing is "sticky" to one machine that happens to remember you.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about REST's three core ideas, per Lesson 2.
options: REST organizes an API around resources (nouns), each addressed by its own URL, rather than action-named endpoints
Statelessness means each request must carry everything the server needs, including auth, even if an identical request was just sent moments ago
REST calls for inventing custom endpoint names like /createUser or /deleteOrder instead of reusing standard HTTP verbs
In REST, a resource's URL changes depending on which HTTP verb is used against it
REST was described by Roy Fielding in a dissertation, and "RESTful" describes an API that follows those conventions
questions.explain: REST's three ideas are resources addressed by URLs, statelessness, and reusing standard HTTP verbs instead of inventing action names. A resource's URL stays fixed — it's the HTTP method that changes what happens to it, not the other way around — and REST specifically avoids custom action-named endpoints like /createUser in favor of POST on a resource's own URL.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: calling a(n) ________ endpoint twice has the exact same effect as calling it once — DELETE /orders/1001 run a second time still leaves the order gone, it just finds nothing left to delete.
questions.explain: Idempotent means repeating the same call produces the same end state as calling it once. GET, PUT, and DELETE are all idempotent; POST is not, since calling POST /orders twice creates two separate orders instead of leaving things as they were after the first call.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Chapters 1's request/response anatomy to what it actually is.
right: A key/value pair appended to the URL after a '?'
The status code plus a short reason phrase, found only in a response
The program handling the request and sending back a response
questions.explain: The client is the program asking the question; the server is the program answering it. A query parameter lives in the URL after the '?' (Lesson 4), while the status line — the status code plus its reason phrase — only ever appears in a response, never a request.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of going from an unfamiliar API's documentation to a real request in the correct order, per Lessons 4 and 5.
items: Find the API's base URL and how to authenticate
Find which endpoints exist and which HTTP methods work on each one
Identify which parameters are required versus optional
Build the request using the documented method, URL, and required parameters
Send the request and check the status code before inspecting the response body
questions.explain: Lesson 5's three things to find first — base URL and auth, the endpoints, and required parameters — come before you can build anything. Only once those are known can you assemble the actual request Lesson 4 taught the anatomy of, send it, and read the status code first, exactly as Lesson 3 and Lesson 9 (Chapter 2) both emphasize.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 6, is this JSON valid? Why or why not?
options: No — JSON does not allow a trailing comma after the last item in an object or array
Yes — JSON allows a trailing comma exactly like a JavaScript object literal does
No — because the key 42 must be written in quotes
Yes, but only inside arrays, never inside objects
questions.explain: JSON's syntax rules require every key/value pair to be comma-separated except the very last one, which must not have a trailing comma. The comma after 42 here makes this invalid JSON — the single most common reason hand-written JSON fails to parse, per Lesson 10.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about JSON's common pitfalls, per Lesson 10.
options: A trailing comma after the last item in an object or array makes JSON invalid
Single quotes are valid for JSON strings and keys, just like double quotes
A JSON number can silently lose precision once it's too large for a 64-bit float, which is why APIs needing exact large integers send them as strings instead
data.get("nickname") in Python returns the same None whether the key's value is explicitly null or the key is missing entirely, which can hide a real difference
A field documented as a string will always arrive as a string on every response, with no null case to ever handle
questions.explain: Trailing commas and single-quoted strings/keys are both invalid JSON, though only the trailing comma is true here — JSON requires double quotes always. Very large numbers can lose precision past roughly 9 quadrillion in a 64-bit float, so exact large IDs are sent as strings. And null vs. a missing key both read back as None in Python, hiding a distinction some APIs care about. A documented string field can still arrive as null for an optional value with nothing set — code has to handle that case rather than assume it away.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the exact path: for {"data": {"items": [{"id": 7}]}}, the path to reach the value 7 is ________.
questions.explain: Reading a path means chaining keys and indexes outside-in: data steps into the outer object, .items steps into its array, [0] steps into that array's first element, and .id reaches the final value — exactly the dot-notation/bracket-notation chain Lesson 7 teaches.

questions.prompt: Match each JSON Schema keyword to what it actually controls, per Lesson 8.
right: Which keys from properties must be present
What JSON type this value must be (object, string, number...)
The value must be exactly one of this fixed list
For an object, the allowed keys and each one's own schema
questions.explain: type names the JSON type a value must be; properties lists an object's allowed keys and each key's own schema; required names which of those keys must actually be present; and enum restricts a value to one fixed list of allowed options. These four keywords are exactly what Chapter 3's tool-calling and structured-output schemas are built from.

questions.prompt: A client calls .json() on every HTTP response immediately, without checking response.status_code first. A 500 response arrives whose body is an HTML error page, not JSON. What happens, and why does Lesson 9 insist on checking the status code first?
options: .json() raises a confusing parse error on the HTML body, which hides the real problem — that the request itself failed with a 500
.json() automatically converts the HTML page into an empty JSON object with no error
The status code is embedded inside the response body itself, so checking it separately is redundant
A 500 response is always valid JSON by specification, so this scenario cannot actually occur
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit that a 500 or 404 response's body often isn't JSON at all — it might be an HTML error page. Calling .json() on that before checking status_code produces a confusing JSONDecodeError that obscures the real, simpler problem: the request failed. Checking the status code first surfaces the actual failure immediately.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of safely handling an API response body in the correct order, per Lesson 9.
items: Check response.status_code before doing anything else with the body
Parse the response text into a real object inside a try/except block
Catch JSONDecodeError if the text turns out to be malformed, instead of letting it crash unhandled
Check that the parsed object has the required fields and valid values before trusting it
questions.explain: Status code comes first, since a failed request's body often isn't even JSON. Only after that do you parse the text into a real object, catching JSONDecodeError if parsing itself fails. Parsing succeeding only proves the text was syntactically valid JSON — validating the actual fields and values, Lesson 8's schema enforced by hand, is the final step.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, what does a 429 response from Anthropic's Messages API mean, and what error type does its JSON body carry?
options: You've hit a rate limit or spend cap; the error type is rate_limit_error
Your API key is missing, invalid, or expired; the error type is authentication_error
Something is structurally wrong with your request body; the error type is invalid_request_error
The requested resource doesn't exist; the error type is not_found_error
An unexpected error occurred inside Anthropic's own systems; the error type is api_error
The API itself is temporarily overloaded; the error type is overloaded_error
questions.explain: Lesson 14's real status-code table maps 429 specifically to rate_limit_error — you've hit a rate limit or spend cap. It's also the one status that carries a retry-after header telling you exactly how long to wait, which is why it's treated as transient and worth retrying with backoff.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F describes 529 (overloaded_error), not 429. Both sound like "the API can't handle this right now," but 529 means the API itself is overloaded regardless of your own usage, while 429 specifically means you personally have exceeded your rate limit or spend cap. Confusing the two matters because only 429 reliably comes with the retry-after header the course teaches you to read.

questions.prompt: Given this raw JSON response with no other context, which API family produced it, and how can you tell, per Lesson 11?
options: OpenAI-style Chat Completions — the reply is wrapped in a choices array and uses finish_reason, not Anthropic's content array of blocks and stop_reason
Anthropic's Messages API — choices is simply another name Anthropic uses for its content array
It could be either family; the two response shapes are byte-for-byte identical
Neither — this shape only ever appears inside webhook payloads, never in a direct API response
questions.explain: Lesson 11's key-terms table draws exactly this line: OpenAI-style responses wrap the reply in a choices array with message.content and finish_reason, while Anthropic's Messages API uses a content array of blocks with stop_reason. Seeing choices and finish_reason together is enough to identify the family without any other context.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about streaming responses, per Lesson 12.
options: Streaming uses Server-Sent Events, with the server pushing event/data pairs down a single kept-open HTTP connection
The event sequence always begins with message_start, which carries an empty content array
content_block_delta events carry the final cumulative usage and stop_reason
A client should ignore event types it doesn't recognize, such as ping
Requesting streaming mode requires a completely different endpoint URL than a non-streaming request
questions.explain: SSE keeps one HTTP connection open and pushes small event/data pairs, starting with message_start's empty content array. The final stop_reason and cumulative usage actually arrive on message_delta, not on each content_block_delta, which only carries small incremental text chunks. Unrecognized event types like ping should simply be ignored. Streaming is requested on the exact same endpoint and body, just by adding "stream": true — not a different URL.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a tool_result content block references the original tool call by placing the matching tool_use block's id into its own ________ field.
questions.explain: tool_use_id is what links a tool_result back to the specific tool_use request that triggered it, since a single turn could in principle involve more than one tool call that each needs its own matching result.

questions.prompt: Match each term from the Anthropic Messages API to what it actually is, per Lessons 11 and 13.
right: Tells you why the model stopped generating, e.g. end_turn or tool_use
Claude's structured request asking your code to call a specific tool with given input
An array of blocks (text, tool_use, and others) rather than a plain string
Reports input/output token counts so you know what the call actually cost
questions.explain: content is an array of blocks, not a plain string — exactly why a tool_use block can sit alongside plain text. stop_reason explains why generation stopped. usage reports the token counts a call cost. And a tool_use block is Claude's structured request for your application code to actually run something.

questions.prompt: An AI provider's batch-jobs list endpoint returns a has_more boolean and expects a starting_after parameter for the next page, while jobs are constantly being created and completed. Per Lesson 15, why is this cursor-based approach a better fit here than GitHub-style page numbers?
options: A page-number offset can skip or repeat items when the underlying list shifts between requests, while a cursor anchored to the last-seen ID doesn't break that way
Cursor-based pagination always returns every item in a single response, avoiding multiple requests entirely
GitHub-style page numbers are not valid JSON, so a JSON-returning API cannot use them
has_more and starting_after are required by the HTTP specification for any list endpoint
questions.explain: Lesson 15 states this directly: cursor-based pagination doesn't break when rows are added or deleted between requests, because it anchors to a specific item's ID rather than a numeric offset into a list that might have already shifted — exactly the failure mode you'd hit polling a constantly-changing list of in-progress jobs.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about webhooks, per Lesson 16.
options: A webhook flips the usual request direction — the provider calls your server as an HTTP POST when an event happens
The Stripe-Signature header's v1 value is an HMAC-SHA256 signature computed from the timestamp, the raw request body, and a shared secret
A webhook handler should complete all of its real database or API work before returning a 2xx, to guarantee nothing is missed
If the signature your handler computes doesn't match the header, the payload should be rejected rather than trusted
Because anyone could discover a webhook URL and POST fake JSON to it, signature verification is optional as long as the URL itself stays secret
questions.explain: A webhook really does flip the direction — the provider calls you. The real Stripe-Signature header's v1 value is an HMAC-SHA256 signature over timestamp, raw body, and a shared secret, and a mismatch means reject, don't trust. Lesson 16 says the opposite of option 3, though: respond with a fast 2xx first, then do slow work asynchronously, or the provider may treat the delivery as failed and retry it. And signature verification isn't optional just because a URL is hard to guess — it's the actual proof the event is genuine.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a complete tool-calling round trip in the correct order, per Lesson 13.
items: Define the tool's name, description, and input_schema, and send it along with the user's message
Claude responds with stop_reason: tool_use and a tool_use content block naming the tool and its input
Your application code reads name and input and actually runs the real function
Your application sends the result back as a new message, in a tool_result block referencing the original call's id via tool_use_id
Claude reads the tool_result and writes a final natural-language answer
questions.explain: Claude never actually calls the function itself — it only asks, via a tool_use block, for your code to run something. Your code runs the real lookup, sends the answer back tagged with tool_use_id so Claude knows which call it answers, and only then does Claude produce its final natural-language reply. This exact five-step round trip is what every tool-calling integration follows, no matter how many tools are involved.

questions.prompt: A request to Anthropic's API fails with a 401. Per Lesson 14, should retry logic automatically retry it?
options: No — a 401 means the API key is bad, missing, or expired, and retrying the identical request produces the identical failure every time
Yes — 401 belongs in the same transient category as 429 and 5xx errors
Yes, but only after first increasing max_tokens on the retry
No — but only because 401 errors are always actually caused by a dropped network connection
questions.explain: Lesson 14 draws a hard line: retrying a 400 or 401 will never succeed, because the request body or the credentials are wrong, not the network or the server's load. Only genuinely transient failures — connection errors, 429, and 5xx — are worth retrying with backoff; retrying anything else just wastes time and calls.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, what's the real benefit of building the API key and headers into self.session inside __init__, instead of passing them to every individual method call?
options: The connection and headers are set up once and reused across every call, instead of being rebuilt from scratch each time, and nothing has to be repeated at every call site
requests.Session() is required by Anthropic's API; calling requests.post() directly is rejected outright
It makes the API key visible directly in every method's own signature, for easier debugging
It removes the need to track a base_url at all, since Session infers the correct one automatically
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit: a requests.Session() reuses the connection and its headers across calls instead of rebuilding them every time, which is both a real performance win and the reason callers never have to remember the key, headers, or shape of the request themselves — they just call client.send_message(...).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about custom exceptions and the retry loop, per Lesson 18.
options: Defining custom exception types like RateLimitError lets callers catch a specific, named error instead of inspecting raw status codes themselves
Putting the retry loop on the client class means every caller gets the same resilience, without copying the loop into every calling script
The retry loop should retry on every non-200 status code, including 400 and 401, since retrying is always the safer choice
It's better for send_message to raise RateLimitError once retries are exhausted than to silently return None or an empty dictionary
continue inside the retry loop ends the function immediately without attempting another request
questions.explain: Custom exceptions give callers something specific to catch by name, and putting the retry loop on the class means every caller gets the same behavior for free instead of duplicating it everywhere a bug could hide. Raising RateLimitError once retries are exhausted is explicitly preferred over silently returning nothing. But the loop only retries 429 and 5xx, the transient failures Lesson 14 identified — not 400 or 401, which can never succeed on retry — and continue skips to the next loop iteration (the next attempt), it doesn't end the function.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on a 429 response, Anthropic's API includes a ________ header telling you exactly how many seconds to wait before retrying, instead of making you guess.
questions.explain: retry-after only appears on a 429 itself, and it's a real number of seconds straight from the API — Lesson 19 has clients read it instead of guessing a backoff schedule the way Lesson 18's plain 1-2-4 second doubling does.

questions.prompt: Match each testing term to what it actually means, per Lesson 20.
right: A slower test that calls the real API deliberately, run outside the normal commit flow
A stand-in object that returns controlled, fake data instead of making a real network call
A fast, isolated test of your own code's logic, with no real network call involved
Makes a mock return a different value on each successive call, e.g. 429 then success
questions.explain: A mock is a stand-in that returns fake, controlled data. side_effect makes that mock return different values on successive calls, which is exactly how Lesson 20 simulates a 429 followed by a success. A unit test is fast and isolated, testing your own logic rather than the real network. An integration test deliberately calls the real API and costs money, so it runs separately, not on every commit.

questions.prompt: Lesson 20's test_retries_on_rate_limit patches both session.post and time.sleep. What would happen if it patched only session.post and left time.sleep real?
options: The test would still pass, but it would actually pause for real seconds during the retry backoff, making the test suite slower for no benefit
The test would fail immediately with an AttributeError before session.post is even called
The retry loop would automatically skip its own sleep calls once session.post is mocked
The assertion on result["content"][0]["text"] would silently stop running
questions.explain: Mocking session.post controls what the HTTP call returns, but it does nothing to the separate time.sleep calls the retry loop makes between attempts. Without also patching time.sleep, the test still passes — it's just correctly behaving code — but it genuinely waits those real seconds, which is exactly why Lesson 20 patches both.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a resilient AIClient in the correct order, per Lessons 17 through 20.
items: Set up shared config — the API key, base URL, and a requests.Session — once in __init__
Write a thin method, like send_message, that posts the real request shape to the real endpoint
Define custom exception types and wrap the call in a retry loop for transient failures only
Read real rate-limit headers like retry-after and back off using the API's own guidance instead of guessing
Write mocked tests that simulate a 429 followed by success to prove the retry loop actually works
questions.explain: Lesson 17 establishes the shared setup and a first real method before anything else can be built on top of it. Lesson 18 then adds named exceptions and a transient-only retry loop. Lesson 19 upgrades that loop to read the API's own retry-after guidance instead of guessing. Only once the behavior exists does Lesson 20 write the mocked tests that prove it actually works — testing comes last because there's nothing to test before it's built.

questions.prompt: A finished AIClient sends the correct request/response shape, has custom exceptions with a retry loop, and reads rate-limit headers — but has no test suite at all. Per Lesson 21's requirements checklist, is this capstone complete?
options: No — a tested retry path, at least one mocked test proving a 429 followed by success recovers, is one of the five required items, not optional
Yes — testing is listed only as a stretch goal alongside streaming and tool calling
Yes, as long as every method on the class has a docstring
No — but only because the class is also missing pagination support, which is the actual missing requirement
questions.explain: Lesson 21's checklist lists five required items: correct request/response handling, resilient error handling, rate-limit awareness, a tested retry path, and clean class design. Streaming and tool calling are explicitly called out as strong additions, not requirements — but a tested retry path is required, so skipping it leaves the capstone incomplete regardless of how solid the rest of the class is.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 22, this course is the third course in the AI Engineer path, and the next course is ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 22 names AI/ML Foundations as the next course in the path — the point where you move from calling AI models through an API to understanding how the models themselves actually work.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about presenting the capstone project, per Lesson 22.
options: The one-minute interview answer should cover what the project does, the hardest decision made, and how you proved it works
A portfolio reviewer is expected to read every line of AIClient's source code before forming an opinion
Chapters 1 and 2 exist so that Chapter 3's real JSON shapes would already make sense by the time they appeared
"I built an API wrapper" is presented as a stronger interview answer than naming the hardest decision and how it was tested
The README should explain design decisions worth calling out, such as why a Session is used and why retries only happen on transient errors
questions.explain: Lesson 22's one-minute answer structure is exactly what it does, the hardest decision, and how it was proven to work. It says a reviewer reads a short README and skims the tests, not every line of source — which is exactly why the README needs to explain decisions like the Session and the transient-only retry policy. And it explicitly calls "I built an API wrapper" a weaker answer than the concrete three-part version, not a stronger one.
